pageTitle: One giant table, cut into pieces

paper.title: Bigtable: A Distributed Storage System for Structured Data

summary: Google had data of very different sizes and needed one place to keep it. Bigtable is a giant sorted table, found by row, column and time, cut into pieces called tablets that live on thousands of ordinary machines. Each write goes to a notebook and a whiteboard, then into sorted folders that are zipped together later. The paper describes its own design and Google’s use of it.

hook.teaser: How do you keep one table when it is too big for any machine?

blocks.kicker: Distributed systems / A picture story in four parts
blocks.title: How Google stored a table too big for one machine

chapters.title: Data of every size
chapters.caption: Many Google projects needed a place to keep structured data. The paper says more than sixty products used Bigtable, from web indexing to Google Earth. Some wanted fast answers for people waiting; others wanted to chew through huge piles in the background. The goal was petabytes spread over thousands of ordinary machines.

media.alt: A small web address tag, a web page and a satellite picture of different sizes all flow toward one big storage shelf.

chapters.title: A sorted map, cut into tablets
chapters.caption: Bigtable is not a full relational database. It is a sorted map: each value is found by a row name, a column name and a time. Rows are kept in alphabetical order, so neighbors in the list are kept together, and reading a short range of rows is efficient. The table is cut into row ranges called tablets, each about 100 to 200 MB by default, and each tablet is served by one machine at a time. Grown-up words: column families, tablets.

media.alt: A long sorted sheet is cut into three pieces; each piece lands on its own desk.

chapters.title: Notebook, whiteboard, folders
chapters.caption: A new write goes at the end of a notebook on disk, then onto a sorted whiteboard in memory. When the whiteboard is full, it is saved as a sorted, never-edited folder and a fresh whiteboard starts. Folders pile up, so the machine zips a few together in the background. A read looks at the whiteboard and all the folders together, and a doorman can say “not in this folder” without opening it. Grown-up words: commit log, memtable, SSTable, compaction, Bloom filter.

media.alt: An envelope goes into a notebook, then onto a whiteboard, then into a stack of folders where a doorman checks one folder.

chapters.title: Thousands of servers in production
chapters.caption: The paper says that as of August 2006 there were 388 non-test Bigtable clusters with about 24,500 tablet servers in total. One group of 14 busy clusters, with 8069 tablet servers, saw more than 1.2 million requests per second. These are Google’s own reported numbers. See Section 8 ↗

media.alt: A big grid of small server boxes, with one group of them highlighted and a counter above it.

panels.caption: Every box in the table has an address: a row name, a column name and a time.

media.alt: A grid with a row label on the left, a column label on top and a clock tag pointing at one box.

panels.caption: Rows stay in alphabetical order. The paper flips web addresses around, so pages from one site sit side by side.

media.alt: Rows of web addresses written backwards sit in alphabetical order, with two rows from the same site next to each other.

panels.caption: Each box can keep older versions, newest first. The paper’s page table keeps the last three.

media.alt: One box with three stacked sheets, the top one newest, each with a clock tag.

panels.caption: As the table grows, it is cut into row ranges called tablets, roughly 100 to 200 MB each.

media.alt: Scissors cut a long sorted table into several pieces.

panels.caption: Each tablet is served by one machine at a time. A machine holds many tablets.

media.alt: Several small pieces sit on one desk with a nameplate.

panels.caption: A master hands tablets to machines, but people ask the machines directly. So the master stays lightly busy.

media.alt: A small manager desk points pieces toward desks while a customer walks straight to a desk.

strips.title: Jot, then pin
strips.kicker: The first steps of a write

panels.caption: First, the write goes at the end of a notebook. The notebook is what lets a machine rebuild after a crash.

media.alt: A pencil adds a line at the bottom of a long notebook.

panels.caption: Then it goes on a sorted whiteboard in memory.

media.alt: The same note is pinned in order on a whiteboard beside the notebook.

panels.caption: One notebook is shared by all tablets on the machine, so the machine writes one place, not many.

media.alt: Three small pieces on a desk all send notes into the same single notebook.

panels.caption: When the whiteboard reaches a limit, it is frozen, and a fresh whiteboard takes new writes.

media.alt: A full whiteboard gets a snowflake tag while a clean whiteboard stands beside it.

panels.caption: The frozen one is copied out as a sorted file that is never edited again. Call it a folder.

media.alt: A sorted whiteboard is copied into a neat closed folder on a shelf.

panels.caption: Reads and writes keep going meanwhile. Now fewer notebook lines must be replayed after a crash.

media.alt: A customer is served at the clean whiteboard while the folder is filed away behind.

panels.caption: Every freeze makes another folder. Too many folders means slow reads.

media.alt: A tall wobbly pile of folders on a shelf.

panels.caption: So, in the background, a few folders are zipped into one new folder, and the old ones are thrown away.

media.alt: Three folders slide into a zipper that outputs one larger folder.

panels.caption: Zipping all of them is a major compaction. Deleted notes are finally gone for good.

media.alt: One single folder on the shelf, and a crossed-out note in the bin.

strips.title: Reading, and a crash
strips.grownUpWords: merged view, Bloom filter, redo points

panels.caption: A read looks at the whiteboard and the folders together, as one merged view. All are sorted, so this is quick.

media.alt: A magnifying glass looks over a whiteboard and several folders lined up as one list.

panels.caption: A doorman can say “this folder might have it” or “not here.” That saves trips to the disk.

media.alt: A doorman at a folder door shakes his head at one folder and nods at another.

panels.caption: If a machine dies, another machine replays the notebook to rebuild the whiteboard.

media.alt: A second desk reads a notebook and rewrites a fresh whiteboard.
